annotations.text: Counter — a design language for the client side

WHAT THIS SURFACE IS

The staff app is a dense work console: steel chrome, 13px type, a hundred figures a screen. It is an instrument.

This is not that. This is the shop's counter, open at 22:00, and its whole job is TRUST — that the price you were quoted in July is the price you get in September, that your balance is not a surprise, and that nothing was hidden from you.

So the language is a well-printed statement of account, not an app: warm paper, hairlines, square corners, real typographic hierarchy, and figures that line up in a column.

Built from the ground up. It shares no tokens with index.html — deliberately, so a customer can never mistake this screen for a staff screen.

THE SYSTEM

Ground #F4F1EA warm linen · Paper #FFFFFF · Ink #1A1714 warm near-black · Second #6B635A · Meta #9A9187 · Rule #E3DDD3 · Firm rule #C7BFB2

Two accents, one meaning each, matched in lightness and chroma:
   #14594A verdigris — THE action. Once per screen, always at the bottom.
   #9B3A22 oxide — money owed. NEVER an action.

Type: Newsreader for every figure and display line (a printed-statement serif with real numerals); Public Sans for the interface. Not Inter, not Roboto, and deliberately not the staff app's Fraunces.

Ramp 11 / 13 / 15 body / 17 / 22 / 34 / 44.
Space 4 8 12 16 20 24 32 40. Radius 4 on controls, ZERO on sheets — paper has square corners. Tap 48.

Depth is hairlines. One shadow in the whole system: the basket bar, because it genuinely floats.

THE ONE DEVICE: the ledger row

No cards. No coloured left borders. Every list in this language is the same row — name and its basis on the left, figure right-aligned in tabular numerals, a hairline between, a FIRMER rule under a total.

That single device carries the catalogue, the basket, the order history and the statement. Four screens, one vocabulary, and it is exactly how a paper statement already works — which is the point: the customer has read this document before.

THE WORKFLOW LAW

One screen, one question, one action.

· The screen title IS the question it answers.
· Exactly one verdigris action, pinned at the bottom in the thumb, on every screen. Zero is allowed (see the Statement); two is a bug.
· Ordering is four named steps — Browse · How many · Check · Send — and the step line is drawn ONLY inside that flow.
· The customer never types a price, a code, or an address they have already given.

WHERE THE PRICE GATE SITS

Sign in carries no price at all, and offers the public catalogue by name: "Browse what we stock — names and photographs only. Prices are for account holders."

Everything from screen 3 onwards shows money, because by then we know exactly who is reading. And the figure is THEIRS — held from the last time we quoted them — so a leaked screenshot is one customer's number, not the price book.

No screen in this language has a place to put a supplier's name. That is a constraint of the design, not only of the data.

THE ANTI-BYPASS MOVE, MADE VISIBLE

The green block on screen 5 is the whole commercial argument in one component: "140 sheets takes about 1,120 roofing nails at 8 a sheet. You have none on this order."

A supplier sells a line. This turns the line into a LIST — and a list is the thing one supplier cannot fill. It is also the only place in the language that earns a tinted ground, which is why it reads as advice rather than decoration.

Same idea, smaller, on screen 4.

NO ACCENT ON THIS SCREEN

A statement is read, not acted on, so both buttons are outlined and the accent budget goes unspent. That is deliberate, not an oversight.

The closing figure is oxide because it is money owed. The footnote invites a customer to challenge a line before it becomes a dispute — the staff app already refuses to hide a disagreement between the debt log and the balance, and this is the customer-facing half of that same rule.

NOT DRAWN YET — say so rather than imply it is done

· Desktop. Institutional and tender buyers will want a wide layout, and the house two-designs law says that is a SECOND design, not a reflow of these.
· Empty states — a brand-new account with no orders and no statement. "Not enough is an answer" is a house rule and it needs its own screen.
· The PIN-entry step between screens 1 and 2.
· Order tracking after Send.

Sample figures throughout are realistic but invented.
If Counter is wrong, these are the other two

Both are drawn low-fi on purpose — they are here to settle a direction, not to be admired.

B · SHOPFRONT is the familiar one: cards, photo tiles, a bottom tab bar, the shape of every retail app your customers already use. Cheapest to get right, and nobody needs teaching. The cost is that it reads as a SHOP — the price becomes the hero, which invites the comparison you are trying not to invite, and the balance and terms become one card among cards.

C · CONSOLE hands the customer the staff app's own vocabulary. Zero new tokens, one system to maintain, and dense tables genuinely suit an institutional buyer. The cost is that it reads cold and administrative to a fundi standing in a yard, and a customer shown the staff chrome will assume they are seeing staff data.

Counter costs the most to build. It is the only one of the three whose shape argues that you are an account, not a price list.
